Stopped
STOPT
v.t. (pret. & pp.)
From Anglo-Saxon stoppian, to close up, to obstruct, ultimately from Late Latin stuppare, to stop with tow. Webster 1828: closed; obstructed; hindered from proceeding. In Scripture two things get stopped: wells, and mouths — and the stopping of the mouth is a courtroom verdict.

Biblical Definition

Paul’s long argument from Romans 1 to Romans 3 ends not with a conclusion but with a silence: Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God (Romans 3:19). The law’s first office is not to reform the sinner but to silence him. Every excuse, every comparison, every appeal to sincerity is closed off, and the defendant stands with nothing to say. Only from that silence can the next verses speak of a righteousness of God without the law, freely by His grace. David had already sung the same order: the mouth of them that speak lies shall be stopped (Psalm 63:11). The word is also literal and hostile. Isaac inherits his father’s wells and finds them ruined: all the wells which his father's servants had digged in the days of Abraham his father, the Philistines had stopped them, and filled them with earth (Genesis 26:15) — the enemy’s work is not to build a rival well but to fill in an old one. And men stop their own ears against the word: they refused to hearken, and pulled away the shoulder, and stopped their ears, that they should not hear (Zechariah 7:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines STOP as to close, as an aperture, by filling or by obstructing; to obstruct; to hinder from proceeding; hence STOPPED, closed, obstructed, hindered.

expand to see more

STOP, v.t. — To close, as an aperture, by filling or by obstructing; as, to stop a vent.

To obstruct; to render impassable; as, to stop a way or passage.

To hinder from proceeding; to arrest the progress of.

STOPPED, pp. — Closed; obstructed; hindered from proceeding; impeded.

Anglo-Saxon stoppian; Late Latin stuppare, to stop with tow or oakum.

Key Scripture

Romans 3:19 — "Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God."

Psalm 63:11 — "But the king shall rejoice in God; every one that sweareth by him shall glory: but the mouth of them that speak lies shall be stopped."

Genesis 26:15 — "For all the wells which his father's servants had digged in the days of Abraham his father, the Philistines had stopped them, and filled them with earth."

Zechariah 7:11 — "But they refused to hearken, and pulled away the shoulder, and stopped their ears, that they should not hear."

Modern Corruption

Romans 3:19 makes the stopped mouth the precondition of the gospel, and every preaching method that spares the hearer that silence has removed the ground justification stands on.

expand to see more

The law’s use in convicting the sinner — what the Reformed tradition calls the pedagogical or second use — is the doctrine Romans 3:19 states. Its practical loss is the most consequential corruption in modern evangelical preaching. Where the hearer is addressed first as wounded rather than as guilty, the mouth is never stopped, and a message of forgiveness arrives for a crime that was never named. The therapeutic vocabulary is precise about this: it can speak at length of what has been done to a man and hardly at all of what he has done before God. But Scripture’s order is fixed. All the world must become guilty before God before the righteousness of God can be received by faith. Remove the first clause and justification becomes an encouragement rather than an acquittal.

Genesis 26:15 describes the standing method of opposition: the Philistines dig no wells of their own, they fill Abraham’s with earth. The pattern holds in doctrine. Error rarely proposes a new source of living water; it stops the old ones with rubbish — a confession left unrecited, a catechism dropped, a text explained until nothing runs. Isaac’s response is the model, and Genesis 26:18 records it: he digged them again, and called them after the names by which his father had called them. That is what confessional recovery is. The 1689 Confession, the catechisms, and the recovery of expository preaching are not innovations but re-digging, and the old names are kept on purpose.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew satham (H5640), to stop up, to shut; saqar (H5534) and atsam (H6105), to shut fast; Greek phrasso (G5420), to fence in, to stop the mouth; sunecho (G4912), to hold together, to stop the ears.

expand to see more

Greek phrasso (G5420) — to fence in, to block, to stop a mouth; that every mouth may be stopped (Romans 3:19).

Hebrew satham (H5640) — to stop up or shut; used of the wells the Philistines filled (Genesis 26:15).

Hebrew saqar (H5534) — to shut fast; the stopped mouth of liars (Psalm 63:11).

Greek sunecho (G4912) — to hold together; the mob stopped their ears at Stephen’s witness (Acts 7:57).

Hebrew kabed (H3513) — to make heavy or dull, used of ears made heavy against the word (Zechariah 7:11).

Usage

"That every mouth may be stopped (Romans 3:19) — the law’s first office is to silence the sinner, not to reform him."

"The Philistines had stopped them, and filled them with earth (Genesis 26:15) — the enemy fills in old wells rather than digging rival ones."

"Stopped their ears, that they should not hear (Zechariah 7:11) — unbelief is an act, not merely a condition."
